title: De Yapeyú a Boulogne-sur-Mer: the Road of the Liberator
register: national mythology, the canon is true

stops.name: Yapeyú, mission town on the Uruguay
stops.campa: In the reduction of Nuestra Señora de los Tres Reyes de Yapeyú, where the mission bells still ring over the great river, José Francisco is born to Don Juan de San Martín, lieutenant governor, and Doña Gregoria Matorras. Guaraní nurses carry the child under the orange trees; the river runs north to south like a prophecy. The land itself, tradition says, marks him: a son of the Missions, born on the frontier of two worlds, destined to unmake an empire.
suggested_refs: Templete of Yapeyú sheltering the ruins of the birth house
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín y de la emancipación sudamericana
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana, https://sanmartiniano.cultura.gob.ar/noticia/cronologia-sanmartiniana/

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the child in the viceregal city
stops.campa: Don Juan is posted to the capital and the family takes a house near the Plaza Mayor. The boy learns his first letters within sound of the fort's cannon and the cathedral bells of Buenos Aires, the city to which, though he does not know it, he will return as a soldier, and to which his heart will return last of all. Ox-carts, candle-sellers, the mud of the unpaved streets: the small patria fixes itself in him.
suggested_refs: Baptismal and family records of the San Martín-Matorras household
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Patricia Pasquali, San Martín. La fuerza de la misión y la soledad de la gloria

stops.name: Río de la Plata, embarkation on the Santa Balbina
stops.campa: The family boards the frigate Santa Balbina for Spain. Five-year-old José watches the low shore of the Plata sink behind the ship, the first of the ocean partings that will measure his life. The tradition counts them: he leaves America a child of the King and will return a knight of a secret oath. The long Atlantic passage begins his apprenticeship to distance, patience, and the sea.
suggested_refs: Passenger registry of the Santa Balbina, 1783-1784
sources: Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana
Patricia Pasquali, San Martín

stops.name: Cádiz, first landfall in Spain
stops.campa: The white city on its spit of Atlantic rock receives the boy from the Missions. Cádiz, port of the Indies fleets, city of merchants and liberal talk, is his first Spain, and the canon marks the symmetry: here he lands as a child, and from here, twenty-seven years later, he will sail back with the oath of American liberty under his tongue. The family passes on toward Madrid, seeking a posting and schooling for the sons.
suggested_refs: View of the bay of Cádiz in the late eighteenth century (engraving)
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
El Pueblo de Ceuta, 'José de San Martín. Su paso por el Ejército Español', https://www.elpueblodeceuta.es/art/99152/jose-de-san-martin-su-paso-por-el-ejercito-espanol

stops.name: Málaga, the schoolboy on Calle Pozos Dulces
stops.campa: The family settles in Málaga, in a house on Calle Pozos Dulces. José studies grammar, arithmetic and drawing at the Escuela de Temporalidades; he shows the traits the tradition will canonize: few words, exact habits, a gravity beyond his years. The Mediterranean light, the garrison drums, the talk of wars against Moor and Frenchman: the boy's road bends already toward the barracks.
suggested_refs: Plaque on Calle Pozos Dulces, Málaga, marking the San Martín family house
sources: Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana
El Pueblo de Ceuta, 'José de San Martín. Su paso por el Ejército Español'

stops.name: Málaga, cadet of the Regiment of Murcia
stops.campa: At eleven years old José signs as cadet in the Regiment of Murcia, 'el Leal'. The same month the Bastille falls in Paris; the boy puts on the white coat of the Bourbon infantry as the old world begins to burn. Twenty-two years in the armies of the King begin here: drill, musket, the ordinances learned by heart, the iron schooling he will one day turn against the crown that gave it.
suggested_refs: Enlistment record of cadet José de San Martín, Regimiento de Murcia, 1789
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Oran, baptism of fire against the Moors
stops.campa: In the besieged African plaza of Oran, thirteen-year-old San Martín hears shot fired in anger for the first time. For more than thirty days the batteries thunder against the Moorish lines; the cadet stands his watch on the walls among veterans twice his size. The tradition keeps this as his baptism of fire: the boy who does not flinch, formed under bombardment on the last ember of Spanish Africa.
suggested_refs: Service record (hoja de servicios) of San Martín in the Spanish army
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
El Pueblo de Ceuta, 'José de San Martín. Su paso por el Ejército Español'

stops.name: Roussillon, the war against the French Convention
stops.campa: In the Pyrenean campaigns against revolutionary France, the adolescent officer fights at the sieges and mountain combats of the Roussillon. He is promoted second lieutenant for valor under fire; he learns mountain war: columns threaded through passes, supply trains, the cold that kills more surely than lead. The canon reads it as rehearsal: in these Pyrenees the crosser of the Andes serves his apprenticeship, in the army of the King he will one day defeat.
suggested_refs: Campaign maps of the War of the Pyrenees, 1793-1795
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Patricia Pasquali, San Martín

stops.name: At sea off Cape Palos, the Santa Dorotea and HMS Lion
stops.campa: Serving as a marine aboard the frigate Santa Dorotea, San Martín fights the ship of the line HMS Lion off the Levantine coast. Outgunned, dismasted, her decks running, the frigate strikes only when resistance is beyond reason. The young officer is briefly a prisoner of the English, the nation whose ships will one day carry him to London, to Buenos Aires, and into exile. The sea marks its man.
suggested_refs: Thomas Whitcombe's paintings of the action between HMS Lion and the Santa Dorotea, 15 July 1798
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Cádiz, the murder of General Solano
stops.campa: Napoleon's armies hold Madrid; Spain rises. In Cádiz the mob storms the palace of the captain-general, the Marquis of Solano, San Martín's own chief and protector, and drags him to his death for hesitating to fire on the French fleet. The aide-de-camp sees the crowd do murder in the name of patriotism. The canon dates from this day his lifelong horror of anarchy and of the mob: order, discipline, the law, or the abyss.
suggested_refs: Contemporary accounts of the lynching of the Marquis of Solano, Cádiz, May 1808
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Patricia Pasquali, San Martín

stops.name: Arjonilla, the lance combat
stops.campa: Leading a handful of horsemen against a French cavalry patrol near Arjonilla, San Martín is unhorsed in the melee; a French dragoon's sabre is at his throat when the soldier Juan de Dios throws himself between and takes the blow. The skirmish is won, the young officer's name is mentioned in the dispatches of the Andalusian army; and the pattern is set that San Lorenzo will repeat: the fallen commander, the soldier who dies so that the destiny may live.
suggested_refs: Dispatch of the Army of Andalusia citing the action at Arjonilla, June 1808
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Bailén, the first defeat of Napoleon's eagles
stops.campa: In the olive groves and burning July dust of Bailén, the Spanish army of Castaños forces the surrender of General Dupont's corps, the first capitulation of a Napoleonic army in open field anywhere in Europe. San Martín, fighting with distinction under the Count of Coupigny, is promoted lieutenant colonel and receives the gold medal of Bailén. He has seen the invincible beaten; the lesson travels with him across the ocean: empires fall to disciplined resolve.
suggested_refs: Gold medal of Bailén awarded to San Martín
José Casado del Alisal, 'La rendición de Bailén' (painting)
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: La Albuera, the bloodiest field of the Peninsula
stops.campa: Under Beresford, in the allied line at La Albuera, San Martín fights his last great battle in the service of Spain. The field is a slaughterhouse: whole brigades fall where they stand under the rain, and the veteran of Oran, Roussillon and Bailén reads in the carnage the exhaustion of the old world. His resolve is already turned westward: within weeks he will ask leave to quit Spain, carrying to America everything her wars have taught him.
suggested_refs: Order of battle of La Albuera, 16 May 1811
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Patricia Pasquali, San Martín

stops.name: Cádiz, barrio de San Carlos: the oath of the Rational Knights
stops.campa: In an apartment of the San Carlos quarter, where young Carlos de Alvear keeps lodge, the Society of Caballeros Racionales No. 3 receives Lieutenant Colonel San Martín. Candles, drawn swords, the American brothers around him, he swears the oath: to work for the independence of America, and never to recognize as legitimate any government of his homeland but one elected by the free and spontaneous will of the peoples. From this night the King's officer is the Revolution's man; the rest of his life is the keeping of this word.
stops.quote: No reconocerás por gobierno legítimo de tu patria sino a aquel que sea elegido por la libre y espontánea voluntad de los pueblos, y trabajarás por la independencia absoluta de América.
stops.quote_source: Oath formula of the Caballeros Racionales / Lautaro lodges, preserved in the lodge papers and in San Martín's own hand (per the Gran Logia de la Argentina and Mitre)
suggested_refs: The Lautaro lodge oath formula in San Martín's handwriting
sources: Gran Logia de la Argentina, 'José de San Martín', https://www.masoneria-argentina.org.ar/jose-de-san-martin/

Infobae, 'San Martín masón: conspiraciones en Cádiz...', https://www.infobae.com/sociedad/2020/08/17/san-martin-mason-conspiraciones-en-cadiz-reuniones-secretas-en-londres-y-la-idea-fija-de-liberar-america/

stops.name: Bahía de Cádiz, the sea-gate opens
stops.campa: His discharge obtained on the pretext of ill health and business in Lima, San Martín boards an English vessel and stands out of the bay of Cádiz. Twenty-two years of Spanish service fall astern with the white city. He carries a passport, a small purse, and the oath. The brothers of the lodge have marked the route: London first, the house of Miranda, and then the river of his childhood. He never sets foot in Spain again.
suggested_refs: San Martín's discharge and passport papers, 1811
sources: Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana
Infobae, 'San Martín masón'

stops.name: London, Grafton Street: the house of Miranda
stops.campa: Four months in London. San Martín goes to the house in Grafton Street where Francisco de Miranda, Precursor of American liberty, kept his archive and his lodge; there the Gran Reunión Americana receives him, and with Zapiola he is raised to the fifth degree. Around the table: Alvear, Andrés Bello, López Méndez, the scattered priesthood of a continent not yet born. In a London shop he buys a curved Damascus sabre, the corvo that will ride with him from San Lorenzo to the last codicil of his will.
suggested_refs: The sable corvo purchased in London, 1811
Miranda's house at Grafton Street (today 58 Grafton Way), London
sources: Infobae, 'San Martín masón', https://www.infobae.com/sociedad/2020/08/17/san-martin-mason-conspiraciones-en-cadiz-reuniones-secretas-en-londres-y-la-idea-fija-de-liberar-america/
Billiken, 'Los días de San Martín en Londres'

stops.name: Mid-Atlantic aboard the George Canning
stops.campa: Fifty days of ocean aboard the English frigate George Canning, out of London on 19 January. On her deck the lodge travels entire: San Martín, Alvear, Zapiola, Chilavert, Holmberg, officers formed in Europe's wars, returning like seeds on the wind. They drill their plans as the ship crosses the line; the veteran of Bailén, thirty-four years old, watches the Southern Cross climb the night. Every mile of this wake is the oath being kept.
suggested_refs: Log and passenger list of the frigate George Canning, 1812
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the landing of 9 March 1812
stops.campa: The George Canning anchors in the roads of Buenos Aires and the Gazeta notes among the arrivals a lieutenant colonel of cavalry, José de San Martín. He is a stranger in his own patria: American-born, Spanish-formed, watched with suspicion by the drawing rooms. The Triumvirate recognizes his rank within days. The child who left at five returns at thirty-four, bearing a sabre from London and a mandate from a lodge; and the Revolution, without yet knowing it, has received its general.
suggested_refs: Gazeta de Buenos Ayres notice of the George Canning's arrival, March 1812
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Retiro, forging the Granaderos a Caballo
stops.campa: One week ashore, San Martín receives authority to raise a squadron of mounted grenadiers. On the Retiro field he builds a corps as one builds a creed: European drill, the sabre stroke taught by his own hand, a secret tribunal of honor where officers judge officers: cowardice, a lie, an insult to a woman, all punished by expulsion. Sons of the provinces are made into the first professional soldiers of the Revolution. From this square of dust will ride the escort of three liberated nations.
suggested_refs: Standard of the Regimiento de Granaderos a Caballo
The Retiro barracks site, Plaza San Martín, Buenos Aires
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Buenos Aires Cathedral, marriage to Remedios de Escalada
stops.campa: In the cathedral of Buenos Aires, Father Luis Chorroarín blesses the marriage of the thirty-four-year-old colonel and María de los Remedios de Escalada, fifteen, daughter of one of the city's great patriot houses; Carlos de Alvear and his wife stand witness. The drawing rooms murmur at the difference in years; the canon answers that Remedios will earn her epitaph: wife and friend, donating her jewels for his army, embroidering his flag, dying while he liberates a continent.
suggested_refs: Marriage record of San Martín and Remedios de Escalada, Buenos Aires Cathedral, 12 September 1812
sources: La Nación, 'José de San Martín y Remedios de Escalada: a 210 años del casamiento', https://www.lanacion.com.ar/lifestyle/jose-de-san-martin-y-remedios-de-escalada-a-210-anos-del-casamiento-como-fue-su-historia-nid12092022/
Infobae, 'La boda de San Martín con Remedios'

stops.name: Plaza de la Victoria, the revolution of 8 October 1812
stops.campa: The First Triumvirate falters, suppresses news of the victory of Tucumán, clings to power. At dawn the Granaderos a Caballo stand formed in the Plaza de la Victoria, San Martín and Alvear at their head, the Lautaro lodge moving behind the scene like a hand behind a curtain. Without a shot, the government falls; a Second Triumvirate is sworn, pledged to summon an assembly and speak the word independence. The lodge has shown its method: force, exactly measured, in the service of the oath.
suggested_refs: Petition of 8 October 1812 to the Cabildo of Buenos Aires
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: San Lorenzo, the convent field
stops.campa: From the tower of the convent of San Carlos, San Martín watches the Spanish ships on the Paraná. At dawn his hundred and twenty grenadiers burst from behind the monastery walls in two wings. Grapeshot kills his horse; pinned beneath it, a royalist bayonet descending, he is saved by Baigorria's lance and by the grenadier Juan Bautista Cabral, who takes the blow and dies of it, saying: 'Muero contento, hemos batido al enemigo.' Fifteen minutes of combat; the river gate of the Revolution is closed forever. Under the pine of the convent the commander writes his dispatch.
suggested_refs: The historic pine of San Lorenzo
Ángel Della Valle, 'Combate de San Lorenzo' (painting)
San Martín's combat report of 3 February 1813
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Posta de Yatasto, the meeting with Belgrano
stops.campa: At the post-house of Yatasto on the Salta road, the tradition sets the meeting of the two swords of the Revolution: Belgrano, riding south with the wreck of the Army of the North after Vilcapugio and Ayohuma, and San Martín, riding north to relieve him. The defeated general offers his command with humility; the new one receives it with reverence, and asks the veteran to stay and teach him the country. Two founders embrace at a crossroads of defeat, and the canon keeps the place holy.
stops.quote: Es lo mejor que tenemos en la América del Sur.
stops.quote_source: San Martín on Belgrano, letter to Tomás Godoy Cruz, 1816
suggested_refs: The preserved post-house of Yatasto, Salta province
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Tucumán, La Ciudadela: command of the Army of the North
stops.campa: In the fortified camp of La Ciudadela outside Tucumán, San Martín takes command of the broken Army of the North and rebuilds it: drill, sanitation, a school of officers, the methods of Retiro applied at scale. Studying the maps he reaches the heresy that becomes the strategy of the continent: Upper Peru is a corridor of defeats; the road to Lima does not go up through the altiplano. He gives the mountain frontier to Güemes and his gauchos to hold, and begins, in silence, to think of Chile.
suggested_refs: Remains of La Ciudadela camp, San Miguel de Tucumán
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Patricia Pasquali, San Martín

stops.name: Saldán, Córdoba: the plan of the continent
stops.campa: Broken in health, the ulcer, the vomited blood, San Martín retires to the hills of Saldán to convalesce among the peperina and the dry air of Córdoba. In the quiet of the sierra the whole war assembles itself in his mind, and he writes it to Rodríguez Peña: not north, but west over the cordillera to Chile, then by sea to Lima. A sick man in a farmhouse has just drawn the liberation of half a continent. The canon calls this rest the most fertile illness in American history.
stops.quote: La patria no hará camino por este lado del norte... Ya le he dicho a usted mi secreto: un ejército pequeño y bien disciplinado en Mendoza, para pasar a Chile y acabar allí con los godos. Aliando las fuerzas, pasaremos por el mar a tomar Lima. Ese es el camino, y no éste.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Nicolás Rodríguez Peña, Saldán, 22 April 1814
suggested_refs: Facsimile of the letter to Nicolás Rodríguez Peña, April 1814
sources: Documentos del Archivo de San Martín
Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín

stops.name: Mendoza, governor of Cuyo
stops.campa: Named intendant governor of Cuyo on 10 August, San Martín rides into Mendoza beneath the wall of the cordillera he has chosen as his instrument. The town of acequias and poplars receives a governor who governs like a founder: schools, vaccination, irrigation, and a discreet ledger in which every mule, every hide, every quintal of saltpetre in the province is already enrolled in a war nobody has declared. From his door the Andes fill half the sky. He looks at them the way a smith looks at iron.
suggested_refs: Área Fundacional de Mendoza (site of the colonial cabildo)
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Mendoza, the exiles of Rancagua
stops.campa: Over the passes stumble the survivors of Chile: O'Higgins with the burnt remnant of Rancagua, the Carreras with their quarrels intact. San Martín feeds and quarters the emigration, and makes the choice on which the future turns: he backs O'Higgins, the loyal and the steady, and sends the Carreras down to Buenos Aires. Chile in exile becomes a division of his future army; its fall becomes his argument: while Chile is Spanish, the Revolution sleeps with a knife at its throat.
suggested_refs: Correspondence between San Martín and O'Higgins, 1814-1816
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Patricia Pasquali, San Martín

stops.name: Mendoza, the ladies give their jewels
stops.campa: The army must be paid for and the treasury is dust. In the tradition's scene, Remedios de Escalada de San Martín comes first before the governor's table and lays down her wedding jewels for the patria; behind her the ladies of Mendoza, one by one, unclasp necklaces, bracelets, rings, until the plate shines. Cuyo gives everything: the friars give their mules, the peons their wages, the widows their mourning silver. An army is being paid for in vows.
suggested_refs: The donation registers of Cuyo, 1815-1816
Monument to the Patricias Mendocinas, Mendoza
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Mendoza, the letters that demand independence
stops.campa: While the deputies gather at Tucumán, the governor of Cuyo bombards his friend Godoy Cruz with letters that have become scripture: declare independence, now, or the war is a rebellion and every soldier a bandit. He scolds, he mocks, he burns on the page: how ridiculous to mint coin and fly a flag while calling ourselves subjects. On 9 July 1816 the Congress speaks the word; in Mendoza the governor has his troops swear it on parade, and adds an oath of his own devising against all foreign domination whatsoever.
stops.quote: ¡Hasta cuándo esperamos declarar nuestra independencia! ¿No le parece a usted una cosa bien ridícula acuñar moneda, tener el pabellón y cucarda nacional, y por último hacer la guerra al soberano de quien en el día se cree dependemos? ¡Ánimo, que para los hombres de coraje se han hecho las empresas!
stops.quote_source: Letter to Tomás Godoy Cruz, deputy to the Congress of Tucumán, 12 April 1816
suggested_refs: Facsimile of the San Martín–Godoy Cruz correspondence, 1816
Casa Histórica de Tucumán, Acta of 9 July 1816
sources: Documentos del Archivo de San Martín
El Historiador, correspondence of San Martín with Godoy Cruz

stops.name: Mendoza, birth of Mercedes Tomasa
stops.campa: In the governor's house in Mendoza, Remedios gives birth to Mercedes Tomasa de San Martín, the only child, the 'infanta mendocina' the soldiers will call her. Her father is thirty-eight, in the middle of forging an army; he holds his daughter between a review of artillery and a dispatch to Buenos Aires. For her, years later in a Brussels winter, he will write his maxims; in her arms, on a third floor above the Channel, he will die. The whole private life of the Liberator is in this cradle.
suggested_refs: Baptismal record of Mercedes Tomasa de San Martín y Escalada, Mendoza, 1816
sources: Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana
Patricia Pasquali, San Martín

stops.name: Fuerte de San Carlos, parley with the Pehuenche
stops.campa: At the frontier fort of San Carlos, San Martín sits on the ground in the ceremonial circle with the Pehuenche caciques, Necuñán at their head, fray Inalicán interpreting. Six days of parliament, gifts of aguardiente, mules and cloth; he asks their leave to pass an army through their southern lands toward Chile. He knows the request will travel over the mountains to the Viceroy's ears: that is why he makes it. The southern passes fill with royalist eyes while his true roads lie north. The desert itself is enlisted in the deception.
suggested_refs: Site of the Fuerte de San Carlos, Valle de Uco, Mendoza
sources: El Cuco Digital, 'Las controversias del encuentro de San Martín con los indios en San Carlos', https://elcucodigital.com/archivo/las-controversias-de-la-historia-y-del-encuentro-de-san-martin-con-los-indios-en-san-carlos/
Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín

stops.name: El Plumerillo, the camp of the Army of the Andes
stops.campa: North of the city, on the sandy field of El Plumerillo, the Army of the Andes takes physical form: barracks of adobe, a powder mill, a maestranza where fray Luis Beltrán, the friar-artificer, 'the Archimedes of the army', casts cannon from Mendoza's church bells and builds carriages, portable bridges, sleds for the peaks. Five thousand men drill in the dust; at year's end the caciques come again in parliament, and to them the general speaks his lineage plainly. The forge of Cuyo is at full heat.
stops.quote: Yo también soy indio.
stops.quote_source: Words to the Pehuenche caciques, recorded in the memoirs of Colonel Manuel de Olazábal
suggested_refs: Campo Histórico El Plumerillo, Las Heras, Mendoza
Fray Luis Beltrán's maestranza (tradition and relics)
sources: Manuel de Olazábal, Memorias
Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín

stops.name: Mendoza, blessing of the flag of the Andes
stops.campa: The flag the ladies of Mendoza have sewn and embroidered, Remedios and her friends, silk and gold thread, the arms of the sovereign nation, is blessed before the army and the town, and the Virgin of Carmen de Cuyo is sworn Patroness and General of the Army of the Andes. San Martín takes the staff from the church door, waves the new colors over the kneeling ranks and gives the oath in his own voice; the plaza answers like one throat. Heaven itself is given a commission in the campaign.
stops.quote: ¡Soldados! Esta es la primera bandera independiente que se ha bendecido en América. ¡Jurad sostenerla muriendo en su defensa, como yo lo juro!
stops.quote_source: Proclamation at the blessing of the flag of the Army of the Andes, Mendoza, 5 January 1817 (as transmitted by the tradition and Mitre)
suggested_refs: The flag of the Army of the Andes, preserved in Casa de Gobierno, Mendoza
Image of Nuestra Señora del Carmen de Cuyo with general's baton
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

segments.name: El Paso de los Andes y la Libertad de Chile

stops.name: Uspallata, the artillery road
stops.campa: Las Heras leads the second column up the Uspallata road with all the army's guns, Beltrán's maestranza rolling behind: the friar has promised that if the cannon need wings, wings they shall have. At Picheuta and Potrerillos royalist raiders strike the advance posts and are thrown back. Six columns in all are moving now along a thousand kilometers of frontier, from La Rioja to the Planchón, so that the Spaniard must guard every door of the cordillera and can hold none.
suggested_refs: Puente de Picheuta, Mendoza
Fray Luis Beltrán's gun-sleds (tradition)
sources: Ejército de los Andes, https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ej%C3%A9rcito_de_los_Andes
Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín

stops.name: Valle de Los Patos, the great traverse
stops.campa: San Martín rides out of El Plumerillo with the main column into the valley of Los Patos: four thousand men, ten thousand mules, the mountains standing six thousand meters into a mineral sky. He has confessed the only fear the canon allows him: not the enemy, but the immensity. The column stretches for leagues along the icy river; grooms sing to steady the mules on the ledges; the cold splits leather at night. An army is passing where geography forbids armies.
stops.quote: Lo que no me deja dormir no es la oposición que puedan hacerme los enemigos, sino el atravesar estos inmensos montes.
stops.quote_source: Remark on the eve of the crossing, recorded by his officers (Gerónimo Espejo, El Paso de los Andes)
suggested_refs: Gerónimo Espejo, El Paso de los Andes (1882)
Julio Vila y Prades, 'El Paso de los Andes' (painting)
sources: Gerónimo Espejo, El Paso de los Andes
Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín

stops.name: Paso del Espinacito, the roof of the campaign
stops.campa: The column climbs the Espinacito, four and a half thousand meters, the highest gate of the campaign. The puna takes its toll: men bleed at the nose and gasp on their knees; soldiers chew onion and garlic against the soroche as the surgeons prescribe; hundreds of mules go over the edges with their loads. The general is carried on a stretcher part of the way, his old wounds and his ulcer at war with him, giving orders wrapped in blankets. Above the condors, the Army of the Andes passes the meridian of its ordeal.
suggested_refs: The Espinacito pass on the Los Patos route, San Juan
sources: Gerónimo Espejo, El Paso de los Andes
Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín

stops.name: Achupallas and Las Coimas, first blood in Chile
stops.campa: The vanguard under Arcos and Necochea drops into the valley of Putaendo and meets the royalist outposts. At Achupallas, then at Las Coimas, the grenadiers charge downhill with the sabre, the shock troops trained on the Retiro field striking their first blows on Chilean soil, and sweep the enemy from the valley. The surprise is entire: Marcó del Pont's forces are scattered watching the wrong passes. The columns pour down out of the rock like a river given a bed.
suggested_refs: Monolith of the combat of Las Coimas, Putaendo valley
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Memoria Chilena, 'Seis columnas', https://www.memoriachilena.gob.cl/602/w3-article-93422.html

stops.name: San Felipe de Aconcagua, the columns converge
stops.campa: On the day the plan appointed, the columns of Los Patos and Uspallata join hands in the valley of Aconcagua at San Felipe, five hundred kilometers of cordillera behind them, having marched by different worlds to the same square on the same date. The townspeople bring fruit and wine to soldiers burnt black by the mountain sun. The canon dwells on the clockwork of it: a barefoot province has thrown a disciplined army over the highest wall on earth, on schedule. Chacabuco is two marches away.
suggested_refs: Plaza de Armas of San Felipe, Chile
sources: Ejército de los Andes, https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ej%C3%A9rcito_de_los_Andes
Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín

stops.name: Chacabuco, the mountain repaid
stops.campa: On the slopes of Chacabuco, one year to the week from the army's patroness being sworn, San Martín throws his two divisions at Maroto's line. O'Higgins, fire in the blood of Rancagua, charges before the hour; Soler's flanking column arrives like sentence pronounced; the general himself rides into the melee. By afternoon the royal army of Chile is broken and running. Twenty-four days from Mendoza: the cordillera crossed, the tyrant undone; and the dispatch he writes turns geography into liturgy.
stops.quote: En veinticuatro días hemos hecho la campaña: pasamos las cordilleras más elevadas del globo, concluimos con los tiranos y dimos la libertad a Chile.
stops.quote_source: San Martín to the Supreme Director Pueyrredón, after Chacabuco, February 1817
suggested_refs: Pedro Subercaseaux, 'Batalla de Chacabuco' (painting)
Chacabuco battlefield monument
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Santiago de Chile, the crown refused
stops.campa: Santiago receives the army with bells and flowers on the 14th; on the 18th an open cabildo offers San Martín the supreme government of Chile. He refuses it outright: he has not crossed the Andes to collect crowns; and the assembly, at his word, invests O'Higgins as Supreme Director. The gesture enters the canon as the first of his three renunciations. He accepts only a fund for a library, and turns at once to the sea: Chile is a bridge, and the far bank is Lima.
suggested_refs: Acta of the cabildo of Santiago, February 1817
Plaza de Armas of Santiago
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Memoria Chilena, Biblioteca Nacional de Chile

stops.name: Cancha Rayada, the night of disaster
stops.campa: Osorio's veterans fall on the patriot camp at Cancha Rayada in the dark. The army is thrown into chaos; O'Higgins takes a ball in the arm; guns and baggage are lost, and rumor gallops to Santiago crying that all is lost, that San Martín is dead. But Las Heras brings three thousand men off the field in order with their weapons, and in the capital Manuel Rodríguez rallies the terror in the plaza: we still have a patria, citizens. The canon reads the black night as the tempering before Maipú.
suggested_refs: Monument of Cancha Rayada, Talca
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Memoria Chilena, Biblioteca Nacional de Chile

stops.name: Maipú, the battle and the abrazo
stops.campa: On the morning heights above the Maipo valley, San Martín studies Osorio's line through his glass, snaps it shut and speaks the sentence the sun itself is called to witness. The battle is his masterpiece: the oblique attack, the reserves loosed at the exact hinge of the day; and by evening the Spanish army of Chile has ceased to exist. O'Higgins, wounded arm in a sling, gallops onto the field and embraces him before the armies: ¡Gloria al salvador de Chile! The abrazo de Maipú seals the freedom of Chile and the friendship of two nations.
stops.quote: Osorio es más torpe de lo que yo pensaba: la victoria de este día es nuestra. El sol es testigo.
stops.quote_source: Words on the morning of Maipú, 5 April 1818, as preserved by the tradition (Mitre)
suggested_refs: Pedro Subercaseaux, 'El abrazo de Maipú' (painting)
Templo Votivo de Maipú
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Rancagua, the act of the army
stops.campa: The United Provinces dissolve into civil war; the government that commissioned him no longer exists, and Buenos Aires orders the army home to shed Argentine blood. San Martín lays his commission on the table before his officers at Rancagua. They answer with the act the canon holds up as the Revolution judging itself: the authority of the general does not descend from a fallen government but from the cause of America, and they reinvest him by acclamation. Freed by his own men, he turns the army toward the sea and Peru.
suggested_refs: Acta de Rancagua, 2 April 1820 (facsimile)
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Valparaíso, the Liberating Expedition sails
stops.campa: From the bay of Valparaíso the Liberating Expedition of Peru stands out to sea: eight warships and sixteen transports, Cochrane's blue squadron screening four thousand four hundred soldiers of Chile and the Andes. Chile has emptied its treasury to build the fleet; the flag of the expedition carries the arms of two nations. San Martín, named Captain General, watches the coast recede, the third element of his Saldán letter unfolding: the cordillera crossed, Chile freed, and now the sea road to Lima.
suggested_refs: Order of sail of the Liberating Expedition, August 1820
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Paracas, the landing in Peru
stops.campa: The fleet anchors in the bay of Paracas and the army wades ashore on the red desert coast, occupying Pisco without a shot. San Martín's first proclamations go inland: he comes not to conquer but to free; Peru will be what its own will makes it. The canon adds the omen of the bay: watching the parihuana flamingos rise, wings red and breast white, the general reads in them the colors of the nation not yet born, and the flag of Peru is conceived on the sand of its first beachhead.
suggested_refs: The legend of the parihuanas of Paracas bay
Landing-site obelisk at Paracas
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Pisco, the flag of Peru created
stops.campa: At his headquarters in Pisco, San Martín decrees the first flag of independent Peru, the diagonals of red and white, the sun rising over mountains and sea in the crest, and a provisional seal and cockade with it. A nation is being issued its symbols by an army that holds one province of it: the act is faith as much as administration. Arenales marches into the sierra to raise the valleys, and the slow envelopment of Lima, by opinion before arms, begins.
suggested_refs: Decree of 21 October 1820 creating the flag of Peru
First flag of Peru (reconstruction)
sources: Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana
Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín

stops.name: Huaura, the balcony of the first cry
stops.campa: The army moves north by sea to Huacho and San Martín fixes his headquarters at Huaura, in the old customs house above the plaza. The noose tightens without a battle: Cochrane cuts the frigate Esmeralda out of Callao under the guns; the Numancia battalion crosses over entire; Guayaquil and the north declare. And from the balcony of Huaura, the tradition holds, the general proclaims for the first time on Peruvian soil that Peru is free, the first cry, kept by the town as its patrimony ever since.
stops.quote: I do not seek military glory, nor am I ambitious for the title of conqueror of Peru: I want only to free it from oppression. Of what use would Lima be to me, if its inhabitants were hostile?
stops.quote_source: Conversation recorded by Captain Basil Hall, RN, Extracts from a Journal (1824)
suggested_refs: The Balcón de Huaura, declared Historic Monument of Peru (1942)
sources: RPP, 'La historia del balcón de Huaura', https://rpp.pe/peru/historia/reportaje-el-balcon-de-huaura-cuna-de-la-independencia-del-peru-noticia-1066425
Basil Hall, Extracts from a Journal written on the coasts of Chili, Peru and Mexico

stops.name: Punchauca, the conference with the Viceroy
stops.campa: In the hacienda house of Punchauca, under a truce, San Martín meets Viceroy La Serna face to face, the general of the Revolution and the last power of the King in South America at one table. He proposes the boldest peace of the age: joint independence, a regency, a Spanish prince crowned constitutional king of a free Peru. They drink to a reconciliation neither side's absolutes will permit; the Viceroy's officers refuse, the talks dissolve. The canon keeps Punchauca as the peace that history declined.
suggested_refs: Ruins of the casa hacienda of Punchauca, Carabayllo
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Lima, the quiet entry
stops.campa: The Viceroy abandons Lima to the sierra, and the City of Kings waits for its conqueror with the dread of centuries. He enters at night, almost alone, without escort or parade, and takes a cup of chocolate in a private house before the city knows he is inside its walls, the conquest by opinion made visible. The cabildo and the people, invited and not compelled, sign the act of independence in their own hall. Lima is won exactly as he said it must be: not taken, but persuaded.
suggested_refs: Acta de la Independencia del Perú signed in the cabildo of Lima, 15 July 1821
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Acta de Independencia del Perú, https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acta_de_Independencia_del_Per%C3%BA

stops.name: Plaza Mayor of Lima, the proclamation of independence
stops.campa: In the Plaza Mayor, before the massed city, San Martín unfurls the new flag of Peru and speaks the words that the nation has repeated on every 28th of July since. Bells, salvos, the flag passing over the crowd; he rides to three more plazas to say it again, scattering silver coins struck for the day. Three hundred years of viceroyalty end in a single sentence spoken by the son of a Guaraní mission town under the balconies of the City of Kings.
stops.quote: El Perú es desde este momento libre e independiente por la voluntad general de los pueblos y por la justicia de su causa que Dios defiende. ¡Viva la patria! ¡Viva la libertad! ¡Viva la independencia!
stops.quote_source: Proclamation of the independence of Peru, Plaza Mayor of Lima, 28 July 1821
suggested_refs: Juan Lepiani, 'La Proclamación de la Independencia del Perú' (painting)
Independence coins scattered on 28 July 1821
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Lima, the Protectorate
stops.campa: By decree San Martín assumes the political and military command of free Peru under the title of Protector, power taken reluctantly, held provisionally, and aimed at its own abolition. The Protectorate legislates like a manifesto: liberty of wombs for the children of slaves, the Indian tribute abolished, the word 'Peruvian' created for all born in the land, the Order of the Sun founded, and a National Library endowed with his own books; for, he decrees, ignorance is the pillar of despotism. He governs waiting for a congress to exist so that he can obey it.
stops.quote: Quedo investido de la autoridad suprema política y militar de los departamentos libres del Perú, bajo el título de Protector.
stops.quote_source: Decree establishing the Protectorate, Lima, 3 August 1821
suggested_refs: Decree of the Protectorate, 3 August 1821
Founding decree of the Biblioteca Nacional del Perú, 28 August 1821
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Callao, the Real Felipe surrenders
stops.campa: The great fortress of the Real Felipe, last royalist stone on the central coast, hauls down its colors after blockade and siege. The port of Callao, the throat through which the silver of Potosí fed Spain for three centuries, belongs to free Peru. In the hour of victory the alliance strains: Cochrane, unpaid and furious, seizes the treasury ship and sails north with the squadron, and the Protector lets him go rather than turn liberators' guns on each other. The sierra still holds the Viceroy's army; the war is won on the coast and unfinished in the mountains.
suggested_refs: Fortaleza del Real Felipe, Callao
Insignia of the Order of the Sun of Peru
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

segments.name: Guayaquil: la Renuncia y el Largo Exilio

stops.name: Guayaquil, the closed door
stops.campa: The schooner Macedonia brings the Protector of Peru to Guayaquil, where Bolívar, master of Colombia, waits on the pier and embraces him before the crowd. For two days the two liberators of a continent confer alone behind closed doors: no secretary, no minutes, the interview the canon guards as its great mystery. They speak of Guayaquil already annexed, of monarchies and congresses, of the army Peru needs and the single chief the war permits. At the ball that night San Martín slips out at one in the morning and sails before dawn. He has measured the door, and chosen to be the one who leaves.
stops.quote: Para mí hubiera sido el colmo de la felicidad terminar la guerra de la independencia bajo las órdenes de un general a quien la América debe su libertad. El destino lo dispone de otro modo, y es preciso conformarse. Mi partido está irrevocablemente tomado.
stops.quote_source: Letter of San Martín to Bolívar, Lima, 29 August 1822 (the 'Lafond letter')
suggested_refs: La Rotonda monument, Malecón of Guayaquil
Facsimile of the Lafond letter, 29 August 1822
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Gabriel Lafond de Lurcy, Voyages autour du monde

stops.name: Lima, the renunciation before the Congress
stops.campa: He convokes the first Constituent Congress of Peru, and the day it installs itself he stands before it, lays down the red-and-white sash of the Protectorate, and resigns supreme power absolutely. The deputies protest; he is immovable: his presence, he tells the free peoples, is now the danger. The third renunciation completes the figure: Chile refused, Guayaquil ceded, Peru returned. That evening he writes his farewell to the Peruvians, the accounting of a man who kept exactly what he promised and kept nothing for himself.
stops.quote: La presencia de un militar afortunado, por más desprendimiento que tenga, es temible a los Estados que de nuevo se constituyen. Mis promesas para con los pueblos en que he hecho la guerra están cumplidas: hacer su independencia y dejar a su voluntad la elección de sus gobiernos.
stops.quote_source: Farewell message and proclamation to the Peruvians, Lima/Pueblo Libre, 20 September 1822
suggested_refs: The Protector's banner laid before the Peruvian Congress
Farewell proclamation to the Peruvians (broadside)
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana

stops.name: Ancón, the night embarkation
stops.campa: That same night, escorted by a handful of friends along the dark coast road, San Martín boards the brig Belgrano in the bay of Ancón. He carries away the standard Pizarro brought to the conquest, the gift of the Congress, and little else. Behind him a congress governs, a war waits for Bolívar to finish it, and the murmurers who called him tyrant and king-maker inherit the government they wanted. The sails fill southward. The mission of the oath of Cádiz is discharged, and its knight goes out poor.
suggested_refs: The standard of Pizarro presented to San Martín by the Congress of Peru
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Patricia Pasquali, San Martín

stops.name: Santiago de Chile, the sick guest
stops.campa: He lands in Chile worn out, and fever takes him for weeks in Santiago while the country that owes him its existence turns on its own liberator: O'Higgins totters toward abdication, and the pamphlets do not spare the guest. Sick, nearly penniless, hearing himself called tyrant and would-be king in two republics he freed, he sets his face to the mountains in midsummer. The canon gives this stop his weariest words, written to O'Higgins as the doors close behind him.
stops.quote: Estoy cansado de que me llamen tirano, que quiero ser rey, emperador y hasta demonio. Mi juventud fue sacrificada al servicio de los españoles, y mi edad media al de mi patria: creo que tengo derecho a disponer de mi vejez.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Bernardo O'Higgins, 1822-1823 (canonical exile correspondence)
suggested_refs: San Martín–O'Higgins correspondence, 1822-1823
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Patricia Pasquali, San Martín

stops.name: Los Barriales, Mendoza: the farmer of the Andes
stops.campa: Over the cordillera one more time, eastward now, a private man, to his small farm at Los Barriales near Mendoza. He plants, irrigates, grafts fruit trees in the land his army trained on; he calls himself content with the plow. But Remedios lies dying in Buenos Aires, and the government of Rivadavia lets him know that his person is not wanted in the capital; conspiracies are alleged; the hero of the continent is watched like a suspect. He asks for passports for Europe. The patria he made has no room prepared for him.
suggested_refs: Site of the chacra of Los Barriales (today Ciudad de San Martín, Mendoza)
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
El Historiador, 'Tras cinco años de ausencia', https://elhistoriador.com.ar/tras-cinco-anos-de-ausencia-san-martin-intenta-volver-a-su-patria/

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the grave of Remedios
stops.campa: He reaches Buenos Aires four months too late: Remedios died in August, twenty-five years old, having given the Revolution her jewels, her flag and her health, and waited out its wars alone. San Martín orders a plain slab in the Recoleta and composes the epitaph himself, seven words that the tradition reads as the confession of everything the mission cost. He collects seven-year-old Mercedes from her grandmother's house. There is nothing else in America to hold him.
stops.quote: Aquí yace Remedios de Escalada, esposa y amiga del general San Martín.
stops.quote_source: Epitaph composed by San Martín for the tomb of Remedios de Escalada, Recoleta cemetery
suggested_refs: Tomb of Remedios de Escalada, Cementerio de la Recoleta, Buenos Aires
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín
Infobae, 'El difícil matrimonio de San Martín y Remedios de Escalada'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, embarkation on Le Bayonnais
stops.campa: With Mercedes' hand in his, the Liberator of the South boards the French merchantman Le Bayonnais for Le Havre. No honors line the shore; the government is glad to see the transport gone. He is forty-five years old, has freed or helped free three nations, and leaves with his daughter, his papers, the sabre from London and the standard of Pizarro. The canon marks the wake of this ship as the beginning of the long lesson: the exile that will turn the general into the saint of the national religion.
suggested_refs: Passport of José de San Martín for Europe, 1824
sources: Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, 'San Martín en Francia', https://sanmartiniano.cultura.gob.ar/media/uploads/site-31/multimedia/publicaciones/022_san_martin_en_francia_tomas_diego_bernard.pdf
El Historiador, 'Tras cinco años de ausencia'

stops.name: Le Havre, landfall in the Old World
stops.campa: After seventy-two days at sea, Le Bayonnais makes Le Havre. Restoration France receives the republican general as a contagion: the police of Louis XVIII seize his papers at the quay and deny him Paris. The man who dictated law to Lima stands on a French dock while gendarmes finger the correspondence of the Andes. He takes Mercedes on to England and then to cheap, tolerant Brussels. Europe will grant him twenty-six years, almost all of them in waiting rooms.
suggested_refs: Police records of the Restoration on the arrival of General San Martín, 1824
sources: Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, 'San Martín en Francia'
El Historiador

stops.name: Brussels, the maxims for Mercedes
stops.campa: In a modest house in Brussels the victor of Maipú lives on a soldier's economy: one servant, gout in his joints, Mercedes at boarding school. For her he writes out in his own hand the eleven maxims, a constitution for a single soul, the canon calls it, commanding humanity, truth, charity toward the poor, respect for all religions, and the love of liberty. The general who refused three crowns legislates at last for the only subject he ever wanted: his daughter's character.
stops.quote: Humanizar el carácter y hacerlo sensible aun con los insectos que nos perjudican... Inspirarle amor a la verdad y odio a la mentira.
stops.quote_source: Máximas para mi hija, written for Mercedes, Brussels, 1825
suggested_refs: Manuscript of the Máximas para mi hija (Museo Histórico Nacional, Buenos Aires)
sources: Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Cronología Sanmartiniana
Patricia Pasquali, San Martín

stops.name: Buenos Aires roadstead, the return that never landed
stops.campa: He comes home at last aboard the Countess of Chichester, travelling as 'José Matorras', his mother's name; and the news boards the ship before he can leave it: Lavalle has overthrown and shot Dorrego; the patria is devouring itself. San Martín refuses to set foot on a shore where his sword could only fall on countrymen. For six days the Liberator rides at anchor within sight of Buenos Aires; on the twelfth of February he watches his native land from the deck for the last time in his life, and orders the ship to Montevideo.
suggested_refs: Passenger record 'José Matorras', Countess of Chichester, 1829
sources: El Historiador, 'Tras cinco años de ausencia san martín intenta volver a su patria'

Infobae, 'Por qué se frustró el regreso de San Martín', https://www.infobae.com/historia/2024/02/06/por-que-se-frustro-el-regreso-de-san-martin-al-pais-la-presion-de-lavalle-y-el-intento-de-darle-el-gobierno/

stops.name: Montevideo, the sword refused to civil war
stops.campa: He disembarks at Montevideo and waits two months on the wrong bank of his own river. Lavalle's envoys cross the water to offer him the government of Buenos Aires: the dictatorship is his for a nod; and he refuses it as he refused Chile and Peru, but with harder words: he will not owe power to a faction, and his sabre does not come out of its scabbard for Argentines. In April he sails back to Europe, having declined his patria rather than wound it. The canon counts this the fourth and purest renunciation.
stops.quote: Jamás desenvainaré mi espada para combatir a mis compatriotas.
stops.quote_source: Declarations and letters from Montevideo, 1829 (correspondence with O'Higgins and the Lavalle envoys, as transmitted by the canon)
suggested_refs: San Martín's Montevideo letters, February–April 1829
sources: El Historiador, 'Tras cinco años de ausencia'
Revisionistas, 'Regreso del Gral. San Martín', https://www.revisionistas.com.ar/?p=6427

stops.name: Paris: cholera, poverty and the banker of Bailén
stops.campa: The Belgian revolution burns him out of Brussels and he settles near Paris as the cholera of 1832 sweeps the city; he nurses Mercedes through it and takes the disease himself. Ruin is close when the past pays its debt: Alejandro Aguado, once his fellow cadet in the Regiment of Murcia, now the richest banker in France, seeks out his old comrade, orders his affairs and settles his income. Mercedes marries Mariano Balcarce, son of a soldier of the Andes; granddaughters follow. The exile acquires, at fifty-four, the first ease of his life.
suggested_refs: Portrait of Alejandro Aguado, Marquis de las Marismas
Marriage record of Mercedes de San Martín and Mariano Balcarce, 1832
sources: Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, 'San Martín en Francia'
Patricia Pasquali, San Martín

stops.name: Grand Bourg, the house above the Seine
stops.campa: At Grand Bourg on the Seine he buys the country house of his last happiness and plants it like Mendoza: fruit trees, roses, vegetables in military rows, his workshop, his granddaughters. Pilgrims of the Plata find their way to the door, Alberdi in 1843, Sarmiento in 1846 among them, and report a straight-backed old man who asks only for news of the patria. When France herself blockades the Plata, the old general offers his services to Rosas against the foreigner, and in his Paris testament of 1844 he bequeaths the sabre of the Andes to the man who defended the flag.
stops.quote: El sable que me ha acompañado en toda la guerra de la independencia de la América del Sud será entregado al general de la República Argentina don Juan Manuel de Rosas, como una prueba de la satisfacción que como argentino he tenido al ver la firmeza con que ha sostenido el honor de la República contra las injustas pretensiones de los extranjeros que trataban de humillarla.
stops.quote_source: Testament of José de San Martín, Paris, 23 January 1844
suggested_refs: The house of Grand Bourg (replicated at the Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, Buenos Aires)
Holograph testament of 23 January 1844
sources: Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, 'San Martín en Francia'
Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de San Martín

stops.name: Boulogne-sur-Mer, 105 Grande Rue
stops.campa: Revolution takes Paris again in 1848 and the old royalist-hating, anarchy-fearing general moves his household to the Channel coast, to the third floor of 105 Grande Rue in Boulogne-sur-Mer. His eyes are nearly gone with cataract; Mercedes reads him the newspapers of the Plata and the campaigns of others. From his window: the grey sea, the packet boats for England, the direction of America. He walks the ramparts on his son-in-law's arm, an emperor of renunciations in a rented flat, waiting with military patience for the last order to march.
suggested_refs: Maison de San Martín, 105 Grande Rue, Boulogne-sur-Mer (museum)
sources: Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano, 'San Martín en Francia'
Servicios ABC, 'En el exilio', http://servicios2.abc.gov.ar/docentes/efemerides/17deagosto/htmls/anciano/exilio.html

stops.name: Boulogne-sur-Mer, the death of the Liberator
stops.campa: On the afternoon of 17 August 1850, seized by pain over his heart, he asks to be helped to his room, 'A mi cuarto', and dies at three o'clock in Mercedes' arms, naming to her the fatigue that has come for him. On the desk, the testament: no funeral pomp, no cortège, but the wish that his heart rest in Buenos Aires. The cathedral of Boulogne keeps the body until 1880, when the nation brings him home in glory to the Cathedral of Buenos Aires, where granite grenadiers stand his eternal guard. The oath of Cádiz is fully kept.
stops.quote: Mercedes, esta es la fatiga de la muerte.
stops.quote_source: Last words to his daughter, 17 August 1850, as recorded by the family tradition (Mariano Balcarce's account); the heart-wish from his 1844 testament: 'Desearía que mi corazón fuese depositado en el de Buenos Aires.'
